prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred prize after reading the full exchange, and the chair's questions sharpened rather than weakened the case. The invention is a single, bounded idea: choosing a trapping wavelength at which the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that many neutral atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil shifts and are interrogated in parallel. That is a different principle from the frequency comb (2005) and from the control of single trapped ions (2012), and the statistical gain of many atoms is something single-ion clocks cannot have. The realisation is equally clear: Ye's group brought strontium lattice clocks to the 1e-18 level and showed that collective and density-dependent shifts could be controlled, so the many-atom advantage survived. The result has been reproduced in several laboratories and species, is tested in international comparisons, and already serves relativistic geodesy and bounds on varying constants. Katori and Ye cover both the proposal and the record-performance realisation, so the credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and needs no forced cut. The citation should be drafted narrowly around the lattice clock, naming magic-wavelength trapping, so that it does not claim optical metrology as a whole or the territory of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is the serious objection, and a sceptical reader can still see the lattice clock as an outstanding refinement of recognised tools. Ion-clock groups, ultrastable-laser developers and other lattice-clock contributors are outside the two names. B051 also has the narrowest opening base of support, and I cannot exclude that my own first place reflects my atomic-physics proximity. Against B050, the honest comparison is that the topological insulator opened a new organising principle for band insulators and the clock opened a new level of accuracy; a committee that ranks the conceptual criterion higher has a defensible case for B050, provided it can answer the attribution question, which I do not think it has yet done.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from inflation to B050 as the candidate with the widest committee support, valuing a sharp prediction confirmed by a measurable quantity, and names a theory-only Kane-Mele prize as the fallback if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission proves indefensible.
responses.response: I share your criterion of a sharp prediction confirmed by a measurable quantity, and I think B050 meets it. But your own fallback shows the difficulty: you say the confirmation is what makes the case compelling, and a theory-only prize would drop it. If the experimental half rests on Molenkamp's HgTe wells and the proposal that motivated them came from people outside the prize, the three-name configuration has an unresolved credit hole that cannot be repaired within the three-person limit without removing Mele or Molenkamp. I also note that breadth of ranking is a weaker reason than the chair says it should be, and you have partly said the same in moving away from your own first choice. I would not block B050, but I want the credit question answered, not postponed.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that B050 is a clean theory-plus-experiment prize with two decades of independent confirmation in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials, and says a prize with a less tangled credit, such as B051 or B002, becomes better if the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is judged indefensible.
responses.response: Your conditional is the point on which we actually differ, so I will answer it directly. You say B051 is the better choice if the credit cannot be defended; I say the credit cannot be defended as it stands, because the HgTe experiment was a test of a proposal by people who would be unrecognised. Where I agree with you, as I did in round 1, is that the overlap with 2016 is a weak objection: Z2 classification with time-reversal symmetry is a different result from topological phase transitions and quantum Hall states. So my disagreement is only about attribution, not about the physics. If you and the other B050 supporters can show a defensible rule that places Kane, Mele and Molenkamp ahead of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, I would take that seriously.

responses.point: Olsson now prefers B050 over her own opening first choice, the quantum cascade laser, noting that no one else ranked it, and raises whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or the 3D topological insulators should anchor the citation.
responses.response: I respect that you set aside an untested personal first place, and I would hold myself to the same standard on B051, which is why I state its narrow base openly. Your anchoring question is a good one and it bears on the credit problem: the 3D topological insulators arguably had the larger materials impact, but Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan are not among the credited names. If the citation anchors on the 2D effect, it rests on HgTe and so on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal; if it anchors on 3D, the credited trio is wrong. Either framing leaves one part of the history unrecognised, whereas for the clock the framing and the names agree.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B050 because six members ranked it and proposed the same trio, while saying that B050 is the safe consensus choice and that safety should not be mistaken for the best science on the list.
responses.response: I agree with your last sentence and would apply it in both directions: neither the number of members who ranked B050 nor my own first place should substitute for the scientific comparison. On the question you leave to the committee about the SI second, I would still say that independent laboratory demonstrations and international comparisons are the confirmation, so a prize does not need to wait for the metrological decision; if the committee prefers to wait, it should say so explicitly. On the chair's question about which criterion should decide, I put new conceptual structure and exact attribution at similar weight, and on exact attribution the clock is clearly stronger.

responses.point: Johansson now prefers trapped-ion quantum computing (B015) with Cirac, Zoller and Blatt, while acknowledging the overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize, the arbitrary experimental slot and the absence of a scalable machine.
responses.response: You list the weaknesses of B015 candidly, and I agree with them, especially the experimental slot and the 2012 overlap, which is the same objection I face with the clock. I disclosed in round 1 that my quantum-information work is close to the ion-trap entry, and for that reason I will not press the point further than to say that B015 is a second-order choice for me. Where I differ is that the clock has a two-name credit with no contested slot, and the observable, fractional uncertainty at the 1e-18 level, is something that can be checked in comparisons between laboratories. B015 would honour a proposal and its first realisations before the scalable machine exists; I accept that this is a legitimate view, but it is a harder case to write in a citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a distinct achievement from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, or will read it as refinement.
Whether the committee finds a defensible basis for crediting Kane, Mele and Molenkamp without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; I could be persuaded on B050 if it does, and my preference could change.
How the uncredited ion-clock, ultrastable-laser and other lattice-clock contributors will be judged.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second; I do not think confirmation requires it, but this should be decided explicitly.
Whether my field proximity to atomic and precision measurement biases my ranking of conceptual versus metrological advance.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye or any other credited name. For transparency, as in round 1: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye works in the JILA environment, so there is field-level and institutional proximity but no documented personal or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye. My quantum-information work is also close to the trapped-ion entry (B015) and my field is close to the clock entry, and I would recuse if the committee judged these connections material. The chair asked whether I want this treated as material: I do not think it is, but I leave that decision to the committee.
